ABSTRACT 
The Cameroon has two bamboo species indigenous to Africa (the alpine bamboo, Yushina alpina

and the savannah bamboo, Oxytenanthera abyssinica), and one largely exotic species, Bambusa 
vulgaris. However, little on their physical characteristics and strength for the composites materials 
applications is known for these two indigenous bamboos species in Cameroon. Therefore, in this 
study, emphasis was laid on the alpine bamboo Y. alpina, to evaluate its potential for biocomposites applications. Y. alpina with ages ranging from 1 to 3 years, 4–5 years, and 7 years 
were characterized. The mechanical and physical properties of these three age ranges were 
compared. In the first place, the surface texture of the fibers was examined by scanning electron 
microscopy. Afterwards, chemical treatment was performed on the fibers with 1 % NaOH. In 
addition, the chemical bonds of the molecules (functional groups) were identified by Fourier 
transform infrared spectra (FTIR) and the thermal properties of the fibers were examined with a 
thermogravimetric analyzer. Furthermore, the fibers density was assessed using the Rilem protocol and a tensile testing machine was used to determine the mechanical properties of the treated 
fibers with 1 % of NaOH. Finally, a dynamic mechanical analysis of 7-year-old Y. alpina fibers was 
carry out. The results indicate that the Young’s modulus of treated fibers with ages ranging from 1 
to 3 years, 4–5 years, and 7 years were around 18 GPa, 10 GPa, and 14 GPa, respectively. In 
summary, this study underlines two primary points: (1) providing a platform for researchers to 
better understand the influence of age on the physical and mechanical properties of indigenous 
bamboo Y. alpina; and (2) providing a platform to validate suitable designs of biocomposites 
materials with Y. alpina.

1. Introduction 
Bamboo is a variety of giant grass widely available in tropical zones around the world [1]. Bamboo is an eco-friendly and renewable 
material and is traditionally used for the construction of housing in Asia, the Pacific Islands, the United States of America, and Africa. 
Bamboos grow rapidly, at a maximum rate of approximately 21–30 cm/day when they are young [2]. In the world, there are over 1500 
different botanical species of bamboo [3]. In the subfamily bambusoideae, around 100 genera of bamboo were identified around the 
world in which 1400 species are reported [4]. In Asia, 900 species were reported, that is 80 % of the world species. Latin America 
pursues the second position by carrying 270 species. In Africa, 40 bamboo species where identified in which Arundinaria alpine, 
Bambusa vulgaris, and Oxytenanthera abyssinica are prominent [4]. Africa has only three known native bamboo species, two of which 
can be found in Cameroon [5]. In the literature, there is very little data on the quantity of bamboo resources in Cameroon [5]. According to Nfornkah et al. the total estimated area of bamboo distribution in Cameroon is 1,215,482.91 ha [6]. It is estimated that there 
are still 4,000 to 5,000 ha of bamboo in the north-west [5]. In the western highlands of Cameroon, bamboo covers an area of 
241,295.87 ha, or 20 % of the total bamboo area in Cameroon [7]. The main bamboo species of Cameroon are represented in Table 1. 
Concerning Y. alpina, to date, there are no data on the quantity available in Cameroon. 
Biocomposites are blends of different materials used for various engineering applications mainly due to their bio-compatibility,

superior mechanical properties, and biodegradability. In the transportation sector, different types of biocomposites are manufactured using bamboo. Various types of components such as interior door panels, sun visors, instrument panels and clusters, etc., which 
are not primarily load-bearing structural elements, are manufactured using biocomposites [8–14]. With regard to bamboo, Getu et al. 
[15] developed and characterized a composite reinforced with sisal and bamboo. The results of this study show that this composite 
reinforced with sisal and bamboo can be used to manufacture automotive parts that do not require very high mechanical performance, 
but do need to be lightweight and recyclable. Other bamboo applications include the Toyota Prius, Toyota Raum and Mitsubishi [16]. 
The aerospace industry also uses bio-composites for its components. The results of the application of natural fibers in aerospace are still 
emerging [17–22]. The use of biocomposites helps to reduce aircraft weight, which in turn saves fuel and is therefore more respectful 
of the environment [23]. A study by Tsai et al. on the Boeing 747-400 and Airbus A330-300, showed that, reducing 1 kg of weight 
reduces carbon emissions by 0.94 kg on the Boeing 747-400 and 0.475 kg on the Airbus A330-300. Thus, reducing carbon emissions by 
1 kg also saves up to 0.3 kg of aviation fuel, equivalent to $1.1 [24]. In addition, Kumar et al. have shown that hybrid composites based 
on polypropylene (PP) reinforced with bamboo fibers meet the need for modern lightweight and strong materials in aerospace [25]. In 
the plastics industry, Bamboo Plastic Composite (BPC) is a new type of composite made by blending bamboo sawdust, or bamboo 
residues, and other fibers as the main raw material at high temperatures. Results show that the composite contains fewer organic 
volatile, indicating that it is a green and healthy composite [26,27]. In addition, results show that bamboo-reinforced plastic composites are durable and resistant [28]. Polypropylene (PP), polyethylene (PE) and polylactic acid (PLA) are thermoplastic polymers 
used in the production of bamboo-reinforced composites [29].

Looking at the scientific landscape, the literature on bio-composites made from Y. alpina fibers is very scarce, or missing, thus, 
hampering advancement of scientific knowledge. Although some attempts have been made to develop different used of bamboo, there 
are no reported comprehensive experimental investigation on Y. alpina (From Cameroon) about the influence of the age on the physical 
and mechanical properties. Therefore, the aim of this study is to determine the age at which bamboo Y. alpina fibers have better 
properties for the manufacture of bio-composites. This information, which will optimize bio-composites production, will be highly 
beneficial to the manufacturing industry. 
After the introduction, the material and method will be illustrated in Section 2, and then followed by the experimental results and 
discussions in Section 3. Finally, concluding remarks will be included in Section 4. 
2. Materials and methods 
2.1. Study design 
The bamboo was taken in the West region of Cameroon, in Bamboutos mountains in Mbouda (Fig. 1). 
The bamboo collected in Cameroon were characterized in France, at the Dupuy de Lome ˆ research institute (DLRI). The collection of 
bamboo species was done with specialists of the International Bamboo and Rattan Organization (INBAR) of Cameroon and the age 
range of each bamboo specie were given by them. Farmers who own the bamboo farm are interviewed to gain the local knowledge of 
bamboo. The age range of Y. alpina were determine by judging the culm color [30]. A comparative study of mechanical and chemical 
extraction methods showed that the chemical extraction methods produced better fiber properties [31]. Costa et al. treated bamboo 
fibers with 5 % NaOH and the Young’s modulus of the untreated bamboo fibers was 8.70 GPa, while that of the treated fibers was 
12.22 GPa. The results of this study demonstrated that chemical treatments improved the mechanical performance of the fibers [32]. 
Therefore, in this study, Y. alpina bamboo plants aged 1–3 years, 4–5 years and 7 years were cut mechanically and the fibers were 
extracted manually. Next, chemical treatment was carried out according to the protocol used by Richmond [33]. Chemical treatment

with 1 % NaOH was carried out on Y. alpina fibers to improve fiber performance.

2.2. Methodology adopted for our study 
2.2.1. Scanning electron microscopy analysis (SEM) 
Y. alpina bamboo from Cameroon, with ages ranging from 1 to 3 years, 4–5 years, and 7 years were studied by Scanning Electron 
Microscopy (SEM) using a JEOL JSM-IT500HR (SEM) at the Christian Huygens research center in France. The microstructure of the 
fibers is analyzed following the procedure used by Nuez et al. [34]. Scanning electron microscope (SEM) observations were made on 
transverse sections of the culm in order to investigate the distribution of the vascular bundles as well as the micro-structure of the 
elementary fibers. Samples are cut out and placed in a mold. Epoxy resin is poured directly into the mold. The mold is placed in an oven 
at 50 ◦C for 24 h. Then, the samples are removed from the mold and the samples are polished with an automatic polisher. Then we have 
metalled with gold to make the surface conductive. The samples are then analyzed using a JEOL JSM-IT500HR scanning electron 
microscope. 
2.2.2. Thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) 
To evaluate the thermal stability, Y. alpina fibers (treated with NaOH) aged 1–3 years, 4–5 years, and 7 years were investigated via 
thermogravimetric Analysis (TGA) using a Mettler Toledo TGA/DSC 1 STARe System. The thermogravimetric analysis tests were 
carried out according to the protocol of Haddou et al. [35]. Tests were carried out from 20 ◦C to 900 ◦C at a speed of 10 K/min under an 
inert atmosphere (nitrogen). The initial mass of the samples varies between 7 and 15 mg. 
2.2.3. Fourier transform infrared (FTIR)

Fourier transform infrared (FTIR) spectroscopy was used to determine the chemical groups present. Y. alpina fibers (treated with 
1 % NaOH) aged 1–3 years, 4–5 years, and 7 years were characterized using a Thermos scientific NICO- LET IS10. The samples were 
deposited directly on the entire active surface of the crystal and lightly compressed with a tip to ensure good contact. The FTIR tests 
were carried out according to the protocol of Lods et al. [36]. 
2.2.4. Tensile test 
In this study, Y. alpina fibers aged 1–3 years, 4–5 years, and 7 years were treated with 1 % NaOH for 30 min. The fiber weight was 
measured on a PRECISA balance. The NaOH solution containing the bamboo fibers was boiled on a hot plate fitted with an IKA 
magnetic stirrer (RCT), and the temperature was measured with an IKA ETS-D4 Fuzzy temperature. The duration of chemical treatment was selected according to the method of Masrat et al. [37]. Afterwards, the fibers were continuously washed with distilled water, 
after which any NaOH solution remaining on the fiber surface was removed and neutralized with dilute acetic acid. The neutrality at 
pH = 7 was checked with a universal pH indicator paper. Finally, the fibers were dried using a brand oven (SALVISLAB IncuCenter) at 
60 ◦C for 24 h. This temperature and time were selected following the work of Masrat et al. [37,38]. Finally, the fibers are then 
preserved in the laboratory at a temperature of 23 ◦C. The tensile properties of dried Y. alpina fibers (treated with NaOH) aged 1–3 
years, 4–5 years, and 7 years were evaluated on an MTS Criterion Series 42. The tensile tests were carried out according to the protocol 
of Maxime et al. [39]. The diameter of each Y. alpina fiber was measured at six different locations along the length of the fiber using an 
Olympus Provis SC 50 microscope. The fibers were glued to a cardboard frame. The frame was then placed in the jaws of the traction

machine. Then, the edges of the paper frame were cut so that traction was only applied to the fiber. The results shown are an average of 
at least 30 validated tensile tests. Tensile tests were performed at 23 ◦C and 50 % relative humidity in a controlled environment. 
2.2.5. Density measurement 
In the literature, different techniques are used to measure the density of natural fibers. Five measurement methods are identified in 
the literature [40]: 
- Linear density and diameter calculation; 
- Archimedes (buoyancy); 
- Helium pycnometry; 
- Liquid pycnometry; 
- Density gradient column. 
There are several methods for measuring the density of bamboo fibers [41–44], nevertheless, there are two main methods: 
- that of ISO 22157: 2019 
- the helium pycnometric method 
More recently, a new method for measuring the density of plant fibers has been developed by RILEM (International Meeting of 
Materials Laboratories and Experts) [45,46]. In this study, we used the RILEM method. In this study, the experimental setup for density 
measurement of bamboos fibers follows RILEM protocol. The RILEM protocol for density measurement setup is clearly explained by 
Ratsimbazafy et al. [46]. According to the RILEM 236-BBM protocol, bulk density measurement involves weighing the mass of a 
quantity of aggregates and measuring the corresponding volume water. The first part consists of determining the mass and density of 
fine sand compacted to a volume of 1000 ml. The fine sand used in the experiment came from Fontainebleau (France), and the weight 
of bamboo particles is measured using an PROVITEQ balance. The entire experiment was carried out at the Dupuy de Lome ˆ research

2.2.6. Dynamic mechanical analysis (DMA) 
Dynamic mechanical analysis (DMA) was performed only on 7-year-old Y. alpina. The instrument used was a DMA Q800 from TA

Instruments; we used the stress/strain method. The DMA tests were carried out according to the protocol used by Ref. [33]. In this 
protocol, the sample is firstly clamped between two jaws. Then, the motor imposes sinusoidal deformation and the sensor measures 
stress. Finally, Measurements are then carried out at temperatures ranging from − 80 ◦C to 250 ◦C, with an angular pulsation of 1 rad/s 
and a strain of 0.03. 
2.3. Data analysis 
The analysis of the results obtains from the experiments realized was carried out using the ANOVA test. The ANOVA test realized 
has aimed to determine the influence of age on the Young’s modulus of the fibers and on the strength of the bamboo fibers tested. For 
this purpose, Microsoft Office software (Excel) was used to perform a one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA). 
3. Results and discussion 
3.1. Scanning electron microscopy analysis (SEM) 
The microstructure of the bamboo section shows the sclerenchyma fibers (see Fig. 2 - a). The pattern of sclerenchyma fibers within 
the vascular bundles of Y. alpina is similar to Kao Zhu and differs from Mao Zhu [47]. Within the vascular tissue, the function of the 
phloem vessel is to transport sugars and nutrients; the xylem vessel and the metaxylem vessel are for the transportation of water. 
Sclerenchyma fibers are ‘sheaths’ and principal supporting tissues within the vascular bundles of bamboo. Fig. 2 (b, c and d) display the 
structures on transverse surfaces of raw Y. alpina bamboo. From Fig. 2 (b, c, and d), the vascular bundles of Y. alpina bamboo are similar 
in shape and remain uniformly distributed. We observe in the three-range age, that the vascular bundles are distributed from dense to 
sparse and from small to large along the radial direction. The results of our microscopic analysis are similar to those of Zhao et al. who 
characterized the 5-year-old bamboo (Phyllostachys) [48]. 
3.2. Thermogravimetric analysis (TGA)

The curves (Fig. 3) demonstrated three-stage degradation. In stage I (25–150 ◦C) weight loss occurred due to the evaporation of 
moisture. In stage II (250–300 ◦C), hemicellulose is pyrolyzed. In stage III (300–350 ◦C), cellulose pyrolysis occurs. This led to a 
massive loss of mass. After that, a slow degradation of lignin occurred. These results revealed that age has no influence on thermal 
properties. Fibers have the same thermal degradation curves, regardless of theirs ages. We can deduce that fibers thermal stability is 
independent of the fibers ages. 
A comparative analysis of thermal degradation curves between Yushina bamboo fibers from Cameroon and those from Ethiopia 
reveals that, there exist similarities and differences that may be due to differences in nutrition and climate. Concerning similarities, we 
can observe that the various curves present three principal degradation stages but their weight loss is completely different (see Fig. 4). 
3.3. Fourier transform infrared (FTIR) 
Infrared spectrum is molecular vibration spectrum. When exposed to infrared radiation, sample molecules selectively absorb radiation of specific wavelengths which causes the change of dipole moment of sample molecules. The number of absorption peaks is 
related to the number of vibrational freedoms of the molecule. According to Fig. 5 (see 5-a and 5-b), the characteristic peaks obtained 
for the common functional groups clearly demonstrated the abundance of cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin. Absorption peaks for 
cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin were obtained and compared. 
Table 2, shows the different functional groups of Yushina alpina fibers obtained after the analysis. The results showed that age has 
no influence on thermal properties. Fibers have the same FTIR degradation curves regardless of age and chemical treatment. 
Therefore, we can deduce that the FTIR degradation of Y. alpina fibers is independent of their age and on the chemical treatment 
applied on the fibers. 
A comparative analysis of FTIR degradation curves between Yushina bamboo fibers from Cameroon and those from Ethiopia was 
performed [49]. A comparison of FTIR curves showed the similarities between Y. alpina fibers from Cameroon and those from Ethiopia.

We observed that the peak temperature is reached between 300 and 350 ◦C. In addition, we have noted that, weight losses are similar. 
In fact, the Y. alpina fibers from Cameroon and those from Ethiopia degrade completely at around 700 ◦C (see Figs. 6 and 7). Therefore, 
we can deduce that the weight loss curves are similar and independent of both bamboo fibers age and the region where there were 
taken from. However, A comparison of the maximum degradation temperature of Y. alpina fibers with other plant fibers showed that 
the maximum degradation temperature of bamboo fibers is higher than that of fibers from other plants (see Table 3). 
3.4. Tensile test 
Following the tensile test, the results were groups in various tables. Tables 4–6 presents the tensile test results.

The results indicate that the aged has an influence on the Young’s modulus of treated fibers. In fact, we noticed that the young’s 
modulus varies with ages. They young’s modulus obtained of Y. alpina fibers from 1 to 3 years, 4–5 years, and 7 years were around 18 
GPa, 10 GPa, and 14 GPa, respectively. In order to determine where Y. alpina fibers can be applied, a comparison of the main mechanical properties was made between Y. alpina fibers and other natural fibers from the literature review. From the density, mechanical strength and specific strength of Y. alpina fibers we obtained, we can deduce that bamboo fiber has the potential to replace 
sisal fiber (see Table 7). 
The response variables selected for this study had been Young’s modulus, maximum strength, maximum stress, and strain at break. 
The hypotheses of interest of the one-way ANOVA test performed had been as follows: 
H0: The means are equals in the groups. 
H1: The means are not equaling in the groups. 
The objective of this part is to evaluate the influence of age on the fiber’s main mechanical properties. This information, which will

optimize bamboo fiber-reinforced composites production, will be highly beneficial to the designers of the manufacturing industry for 
making bio-composites. Tables 8–11 showed the results of the ANOVA analysis. 
In the ANOVA analysis, the null hypothesis is that the group means are all equal, and the alternative hypothesis is that they are not. 
A big F (in the one-way ANOVA analysis), with a small p-value, means that the null hypothesis is discredited, and we would assert that 
the means are significantly different (while a small F, with a big p-value indicates that they are not significantly different). 
According to Tables 8–10 we notice that we have a small F, with a big p-value. Therefore, we accept H0 because we do not have 
statistically significant evidence at α = 0.05 to show that there is a difference in mean between the three groups. This means that the 
three groups are not significantly different. In conclusion, the age of Y. alpina bamboo fibers has no significant effect on the following 
three parameters: Young’s modulus, maximum force and peak stress. This conclusion is confirmed by the curves in Figs. 8 and 9 (see 
Fig. 8-a; 8-c; 8-d; 9-a; 9-b; 9-c); 
However, Table 11 shows a large F, with a small p-value. We reject H0 because we have statistically significant evidence at α = 0.05 
to show that there is a difference in mean between the three groups. In conclusion, the age of Y. alpina bamboo fibers has a significant 
effect on deformation at break (see Fig. 8-b). 
Our results were compared with those in the literature. Wang et al. [51] found that the average tensile modulus of Ma bamboo 
(Dendrocalamus latiflorus Munro) fibers at 4 years of age were 45.8 GPa, significantly higher than the 34.6 GPa recorded for Moso 
Bamboo (Phyllostachys edulis) of the same age [52]. In Moso bamboo, it has been found that the tensile modulus and strength of fibers

varies very little across samples ranging from 0.5 to 4 years in age, thereby indicating that age has little effect on mechanical properties 
at the cell wall level after the first 6 months [52]. Huang et al. [53] have also studied the effect of bamboo age (0.5–8.5 years) on the 
mechanical properties of Moso bamboo fibers, and their results have indicated that there is no significant variation in average tensile 
modulus and fracture strain. Ren et al. [54] have evaluated the effect of age on the fiber tensile mechanical properties of two 
commercially important bamboo species of China, namely Lv bamboo (Dendrocalamopsis oldhami) and Ma bamboo. The results of their 
work have demonstrated that the bamboo age has little effect on tensile modulus and tensile strength in both Lv bamboo and Ma 
bamboo fibers (see Fig. 10). 
Therefore, in terms of their mechanical properties, Y. alpina fibers appear to be an ideal choice for fabrication of fiber-reinforced 
composites. In conclusion, in terms of reinforcement effect, 1-3-year-old Y. alpina bamboo fibers could be used to fabricate fiberreinforced composites. 
3.5. Density measurement 
Density measurement results (Table 13) show significant variations which can be related to the measurement method. The RILEM 
protocol requires less sophisticated equipment, nevertheless the Rilem protocol is time-consuming, and the test must be repeated many 
times to reach the desired density range (see Table 12). 
The density and the mechanical properties of the fibers determine their potential applications. In order to determine where the 
fibers can be applied, a comparison was made between Y. alpina fibers and other natural fibers (Table 14). From the density, mechanical strength and specific strength of Y. alpina fibers we obtained, we can deduce that bamboo fiber has the potential to replace 
sisal fibers. Table 15 shows the potential applications of other fibers. Therefore, Y. alpina can be used to manufacture composites, 
furniture materials, textile and bags. 
3.6. Dynamic mechanical analysis (DMA) 
Dynamic mechanical analysis (DMA) method is used to measure viscoelastic properties such as storage and loss moduli of materials.

Fig. 11 shows the results of the DMA analysis. The green curve represents the storage modulus (E′). The brown curve represents the loss 
modulus. The loss modulus (E″) describes the energy dissipated (lost as heat) during a stress cycle in the material. The blue curve 
represents the damping factor (tan delta). Tan delta corresponds to the ratio of the elastic (E′) to the viscous (E″) properties. These 
different moduli are translated by Young’s complex modulus equation. The complex Young’s modulus is defined as the vectorial sum of 
the Young’s modulus (E′, real part) and the loss modulus (E″, imaginary part) [56]: 
E* = E’ + i E" 
The E′ reflected the rigidity which was closely correlated with the load bearing capacity of the fibers. If the storage modulus is

higher than the loss modulus, the material can be regarded as mainly elastic. From Fig. 5, The E’ has not verily significantly decreased 
with the increase of temperature from − 70 to 250 ◦C, which was correlated to the chemical treatment. It showed that, the chemical 
treatment has a positive impact on the fibers. In addition, the storage modulus is higher than the loss modulus from − 80 ◦C to 200 ◦C. 
We can deduce that the fibers are mainly elastic in that range (− 80 ◦C–200 ◦C). 
The curves of the loss modulus (E″) and the damping factor (tan delta) are similar. The curves (loss modulus and tan delta) 
demonstrated four-stage. In stage I (− 80 ◦C to − 65 ◦C) we observed a slightly decrease, then in stage II (− 65 ◦C–30 ◦C) we observe an 
increase up to the first peak. In addition, in stage III (30 ◦C–150 ◦C), we observe a rapid decay of the curve up to the second minimum. 
In the last stage (150 ◦C–250 ◦C), the thermal movement of the molecules became evident, and we observe a very rapid curve growth to 
the maximum point.

4. Conclusion 
In conclusion, we can affirm that, Y. alpina fibers have a potential reinforcement for the manufacture of bio-composites. Beyond its 
traditional application, Y. alpina has potential applications in the textile sectors, and composite. The TGA results showed that the fiber 
thermal stability is independent of fiber age. The FTIR results showed that age has no influence on thermal properties. Fibers have the 
same FTIR degradation curves regardless of age and chemical treatment. The mechanical behaviors of Y. alpina fibers depend on their 
source, age and location. Therefore, in terms of reinforcement effect, 1-3-year-old Y. alpina bamboo fibers could be used to fabricate 
fiber-reinforced composites. Future studies should aim to incorporate a more diverse range of bamboos samples to account for potential variations in composition and properties.
